# Saga

> Saga is a multi-agent chat harness. You mention Claude Code, Codex, Grok or an API model with `@name`, and one user-specific Walrus namespace stores their shared knowledge. These steps build it from source and run it on this machine. Use Linux or macOS. On Windows, use Ubuntu inside WSL2. Run the steps in order, from the repository root. If a command fails, fix that step before you continue. Each step says what success looks like.

You do not need a wallet, a Walrus account or an API key to build, test or open the UI. A real chat response requires an authenticated CLI or an API key. Walrus persistence separately requires the MemWal keys. The first build downloads pinned dependencies from GitHub, so you need a network connection. Keep existing .env files, provider logins and saga.json settings; do not replace them to follow this guide.

## 1. Install the toolchain

You need git, CMake 3.24 or newer, and a C++23 compiler (GCC 13 or newer, or Apple Clang). Python 3 runs the smoke check. Use Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian 13+, or a current Fedora release; older distributions may supply an incompatible compiler or CMake.

Debian or Ubuntu, including Ubuntu on WSL2:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install cmake ninja-build g++ binutils libcurl4-openssl-dev libsodium-dev zlib1g-dev git pkg-config curl python3
```

Fedora:

```bash
sudo dnf install cmake ninja-build gcc-c++ binutils libcurl-devel libsodium-devel zlib-devel git pkgconf curl python3
```

macOS, with Homebrew (git, curl and zlib come with the system):

```bash
brew install cmake ninja libsodium pkgconf python
```

Windows: run `wsl --install` in PowerShell and open Ubuntu. Do every step inside Ubuntu, including installing the agent CLIs in step 6.

## 2. Clone

```bash
git clone https://github.com/dun999/Saga.git
cd Saga
```

Stay in this directory for every step below. This file is `llms.txt` in the checkout.

## 3. Build

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build --parallel 2
```

Success: `./build/saga` and `./build/saga_memory_tests` exist. Run `ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure` to check shared memory against a local relayer fixture; this needs no keys and writes nothing to mainnet.

If the build fails:

- `unknown pseudo-op: .base64`: an old assembler was found before the one your compiler expects. GCC 15 or newer needs binutils 2.43 or newer. `command -v as` should print `/usr/bin/as` when using the distro compiler. Put the system binaries first and reset the CMake cache:

  ```bash
  export PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH
  cmake --fresh -S . -B build -G Ninja
  cmake --build build --parallel 2
  ```

  Add `/usr/bin` to the front of `PATH` and keep the rest. The `claude`, `codex` and `grok` CLIs often live in `~/.local/bin`, and Saga finds them through this shell's `PATH`.
- `Killed` or `signal 9` while compiling: the machine ran out of memory. Retry with `cmake --build build --parallel 1`.

## 4. Check the build

```bash
./build/saga help
python3 tests/local/smoke.py ./build/saga
```

Success: help starts with `saga — multi-agent harness with shared Walrus Memory`, followed by the command list. The smoke check prints `Local smoke checks passed` after checking startup, embedded assets (including this file), guest login, missing-key errors, terminal chat and a successful streamed turn using a local provider fixture. It isolates credentials and installed CLIs, creates temporary workspaces, and cleans up its servers. No real model or Walrus calls are made.

## 5. Serve the UI without keys

```bash
./build/saga serve --no-memory
```

Success: it prints `saga: listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` and keeps running in the foreground until you press Ctrl+C. If you are an agent driving a shell, retain the PID and check that this server started (not just another process on the same port):

```bash
saga_log=$(mktemp /tmp/saga-serve.XXXXXX)
./build/saga serve --no-memory > "$saga_log" 2>&1 &
saga_pid=$!
sleep 2
kill -0 "$saga_pid" && curl -fsS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8080/app
```

That check should print `200`. On failure, read `cat "$saga_log"`. Stop this background server with `kill "$saga_pid"` before restarting with different settings; do not kill an unrelated process using the port.

Expected messages that are not bugs:

- `--no-memory` is required until step 7. Without it, `serve` exits with `saga: MEMWAL_PRIVATE_KEY and MEMWAL_ACCOUNT_ID must be set (see .env.example)`.
- `saga: cannot listen on 127.0.0.1:8080 (already in use? pick another with --port)` means another program is using that port. Add `--port 8081` and use that port in the URLs below.

In a browser:

- http://127.0.0.1:8080/ is the landing page. **Start chatting** opens the app.
- http://127.0.0.1:8080/app asks for a guest name. Type any name and press **Continue as guest**. The sidebar shows the name, and the page says memory is off.
- http://127.0.0.1:8080/llms.txt is this file.

What happens when you send a message:

| Message | Result |
|---|---|
| `@claude hello`, with Claude Code installed and signed in (step 6) | Claude replies. |
| `@claude hello`, without the CLI | Saga reports `claude not found on PATH` and hands the turn to `@saga`. |
| `hello`, with no mention | The turn goes to `@saga`. It fails with `BOUNDLESS_API_KEY not set` until step 7. |

`serve` reads `saga.json` and `.env` from the current directory and keeps chat workspaces in `workspaces/`. On `127.0.0.1` it uses the CLI logins of the user who started it.

## 6. Agents you can mention

`saga.json` defines the teammates:

- `@claude` is the Claude Code CLI (`claude`).
- `@codex` is the Codex CLI (`codex`).
- `@grok` is the Grok CLI (`grok`).
- `@saga` is an API model that needs `BOUNDLESS_API_KEY` (step 7).

Install and sign in only the CLIs you want, following each provider's instructions. Then restart `serve` from a shell where `command -v claude` (or `codex`, or `grok`) prints a path. A missing CLI is shown as unavailable, and the server still runs.

## 7. Optional: @saga and Walrus memory

Get the keys:

- `MEMWAL_PRIVATE_KEY` and `MEMWAL_ACCOUNT_ID` from https://memory.walrus.xyz
- `BOUNDLESS_API_KEY` from https://inference.boundless.network

```bash
test -e .env || cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env`; the command above preserves an existing file. Put each value alone on its line. Saga keeps every character after `=`, so a `# comment` on the same line becomes part of the key and breaks it. Set only `BOUNDLESS_API_KEY` if you want `@saga` with memory off; set both MemWal variables to enable persistence.

```dotenv
MEMWAL_PRIVATE_KEY=suiprivkey1...
MEMWAL_ACCOUNT_ID=0x...
BOUNDLESS_API_KEY=...
```

A variable already set in the environment overrides `.env`. Empty MemWal values still fail with the MEMWAL message from step 5 unless `--no-memory` is present. Stop the server from step 5 before restarting it. For `@saga` alone, restart `./build/saga serve --no-memory` and send `hello`.

For real Walrus memory, set both MemWal keys and run the following. `doctor` writes a real probe to Walrus mainnet and recalls it; it is not a credential-free test.

```bash
./build/saga doctor
```

Success: the relayer, network, delegate key, `remember → Walrus blob` and `recall` lines all say `ok`, and the output ends with a walruscan.com link to the test blob. Agents you have not installed show as unavailable. That does not fail `doctor`.

Then serve with memory:

```bash
./build/saga serve
```

## 8. Terminal chat, without a browser

```bash
./build/saga chat --user mira --no-memory
```

`/quit` exits. With memory on (drop `--no-memory` after step 7), `/good` and `/bad <reason>` rate the last turn. A feedback comment is queued as shared knowledge; the foundation prompt stays fixed. An agent can drive it through a pipe:

```bash
printf '@claude reply with: ok\n/quit\n' | ./build/saga chat --user mira --no-memory
```

## Serving other people

Keep this setup on `127.0.0.1`. Serving another host needs Linux and `--accounts user --public-origin https://… --agent-cgroups PATH`. Sign-in is then a wallet, or a username with a password (`--wallet-only` allows wallets only). The README and `deploy/saga.service` cover that setup.
